title: THE OLD TESTAMENT MARRIAGES WE WOULD RATHER NOT TALK ABOUT
paragraphs:
THE OLD TESTAMENT MARRIAGES WE WOULD RATHER NOT TALK ABOUT
They loved, betrayed, waited, manipulated, endured, failed, forgave, and sometimes shattered one another—and buried inside their complicated marriages is a warning modern Christians desperately need before we confuse what the Bible records with what God approves.
Somewhere tonight, a husband and wife will lie inches apart in the same bed and feel miles away from each other.
Someone will stare at a wedding photograph and wonder where those two smiling people went.
Someone will discover a message that was never supposed to be discovered.
Someone will whisper, “I forgive you,” while wondering whether trust can ever breathe again.

Someone else will remain in a relationship where the word “submission” has been weaponized against them, and they have been made to believe that enduring cruelty without seeking help is somehow holiness.
And somewhere, a single Christian will read another beautiful marriage testimony online and quietly ask God, “Why hasn’t that happened for me?”
Then we open the Old Testament.
And surprisingly, we do not find a collection of spotless marriages posing for religious photographs.
We find Adam blaming Eve.
Abraham and Sarah carrying promises from God while also carrying fear, impatience, cultural pressures, and the devastating consequences surrounding Hagar.
We find Isaac and Rebekah beginning with tenderness but eventually inhabiting a household fractured by favoritism and deception.
We find Jacob loving Rachel, Leah aching to be loved, two sisters trapped inside a family structure filled with rivalry, jealousy, children, servants, bargaining, and heartbreak.
We find David accumulating wives while his household slowly becomes a place of sexual sin, violence, rivalry, grief, and bloodshed.
We find Solomon—the king famous for wisdom—allowing his many marriages to become part of his spiritual downfall.
This is where some readers make a dangerous mistake.
They assume that because something happened in the Bible, God must have approved of it.
He did not.
The Bible is sometimes brutally honest precisely because God refuses to edit human sin out of the story.
Scripture is not embarrassed by broken people.
It exposes them.
And perhaps that is one reason these ancient marriages still feel disturbingly modern.
Because underneath the tents, livestock, royal palaces, arranged unions, inheritance customs, and ancient Near Eastern social structures were human hearts.
Hearts like ours.
Hearts that wanted to be chosen.
Hearts terrified of rejection.
Hearts capable of extraordinary faithfulness and astonishing selfishness.
Hearts that could love someone in the morning and wound them before nightfall.

And if we read these marriages carefully—not merely asking, “What did these people do?” but, “What does the whole counsel of Scripture reveal about what God intended?”—something extraordinary begins to emerge.
The first marriage appears before sin enters the human story.
Before adultery.
Before divorce.
Before jealousy.
Before polygamy.
Before domestic manipulation.
Before husbands and wives learned how to hide from each other.
Genesis takes us back to the beginning.
After God creates the woman and brings her to the man, Adam responds with words of recognition and belonging:
“Bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.”
Then Genesis 2:24 gives the foundational pattern:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew is worth slowing down for.
The verb דָּבַק — dabaq — carries the sense of clinging, holding fast, remaining closely joined.
And then comes:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Marriage in the biblical vision is not merely two people sharing an address, a surname, expenses, children, or physical intimacy.
It is covenantal union.
That does not mean spouses cease to be individual persons. It means marriage creates a profound relational union characterized by faithfulness, belonging, and covenant commitment.
And notice something important.
Genesis gives us this pattern before the Bible gives us the disasters.
That matters.

Because when later generations multiply wives, practice favoritism, commit adultery, exploit power, deceive one another, or fracture their households, those stories must be read against God’s creational design—not used to rewrite it.
Consider Abraham and Sarah.
Their story contains magnificent faith.
It also contains fear.
God had promised Abraham descendants, yet the waiting became unbearable.
Genesis 16 records Sarah giving Hagar to Abraham according to a practice understandable within their ancient cultural world.
But culturally understandable does not mean spiritually ideal.
Human beings have always been tempted to “help” God fulfill promises on our timetable.
That temptation did not die with Abraham.
Modern Christians do it too.
We pray.
We wait.
Nothing changes.
Then anxiety begins preaching.
“God is taking too long.”
“You need to fix this yourself.”
“You cannot trust Him with this.”
“Take control.”
And sometimes the greatest damage in a marriage does not begin with hatred.
It begins with fear.
Fear of never having children.
Fear of losing financial security.
Fear that our spouse will leave.
Fear that we married the wrong person.
Fear that God has forgotten us.
Fear makes terrible decisions look reasonable.
Abraham and Sarah teach us that a marriage can belong to people of genuine faith and still contain moments of catastrophic human weakness.
That should humble every Christian couple.
Being believers does not make us incapable of damaging each other.
We still need repentance.
We still need wisdom.
We still need accountability.
We still need grace.
Then there is Isaac and Rebekah.
Their early story contains one of Scripture’s tender descriptions: Isaac loved Rebekah.
But years later their family became divided.
Isaac favored Esau.
Rebekah favored Jacob.
Favoritism became fertile soil for secrecy.
Secrecy produced manipulation.
Manipulation deepened division.
Eventually a son fled from home.
How many modern families understand that pattern?
Not necessarily because one parent literally chooses one child over another, but because alliances begin forming inside the home.
Mom tells the daughter what she refuses to tell Dad.
Dad makes the son his emotional confidant against Mom.
One parent becomes “the good one.”
The other becomes “the problem.”
Children learn how to navigate the tension.
Soon the family is technically together while emotionally divided into teams.
The house still stands.
But covenant intimacy is bleeding behind the walls.
Then Jacob enters one of the saddest marriage stories in Genesis.
He loves Rachel.
But through Laban’s deception, he first receives Leah.
Eventually the household expands into a painful web involving Rachel, Leah, Bilhah, and Zilpah.
Read those chapters slowly and you will hear something deeper than ancient genealogy.
You will hear a woman desperate to be loved.
After Leah bears Reuben, Genesis 29:32 records her hope that perhaps now her husband will love her.
Then another son.
Then another.
There is something almost unbearable about watching a human being try to earn affection through performance.
Maybe now he will love me.
Maybe now she will respect me.
Maybe if I earn more.
Maybe if I lose weight.
Maybe if I become more agreeable.
Maybe if I never complain.
Maybe if I give him sex whenever he wants it.
Maybe if I become more spiritual.
Maybe if I serve harder.
Maybe if I stop needing anything.
Maybe then I will finally be enough.
But marriage was never designed to answer the deepest question of human worth.
Your spouse cannot carry the weight of being your savior.
Only Christ can.

That does not excuse emotional neglect. Husbands and wives are commanded to love faithfully. But if your entire identity depends upon another fallen human being constantly proving your worth, even a loving marriage will eventually collapse beneath expectations it was never created to bear.
And this is where the Gospel begins reaching into places marriage advice cannot reach.
Because Christianity does not ultimately say, “Find the perfect person who will finally make you whole.”
It says that reconciliation with God comes through Jesus Christ.
Before you are somebody’s husband or wife…
before you are single, divorced, widowed, rejected, betrayed, desired, unwanted, happily married, or barely holding your marriage together…
your deepest problem is sin, and your deepest need is Christ.
That changes how we read David.
David is one of Scripture’s most sobering warnings against romanticizing biblical heroes.
He was Israel’s celebrated king.
He was also capable of horrific sexual and moral failure.
Second Samuel 11 records his taking Bathsheba and arranging the death of her husband Uriah.
Whatever sentimental versions of the story modern culture sometimes creates, the biblical narrative is dark.
David possessed royal power.
Uriah died because David abused it.
Then Nathan confronted him.
“You are the man.”
David’s response in 2 Samuel 12:13 is painfully brief:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
Psalm 51 opens a window into the repentance associated with David’s sin:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Notice what repentance does not sound like.
“I was lonely.”
“My marriage wasn’t meeting my needs.”
“She understood me.”
“He made me feel alive again.”
“We never meant for anyone to get hurt.”
“God knows my heart.”
Repentance stops editing the confession.
“I have sinned.”
That sentence can become the doorway through which grace enters a dying marriage.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
David was forgiven, but his actions still produced terrible consequences.
Biblical grace is not God pretending sin did not matter.
Grace is costly.
And nowhere do we see its cost more clearly than at the cross.
But before we arrive there, Solomon gives us another warning.
First Kings 11 says Solomon loved many foreign women and accumulated hundreds of wives and concubines. The text specifically explains that his wives turned his heart after other gods.
The central issue in the biblical warning is covenant unfaithfulness and idolatry.

This matters when Christians discuss Old Testament restrictions concerning intermarriage. The biblical concern cannot responsibly be reduced to modern racial categories. Scripture’s theological concern was Israel’s covenant loyalty to the LORD and the danger of being drawn into idolatry.
Solomon had wisdom.
But possessing wisdom is not the same as obeying wisdom.
That should frighten anyone who knows enough Bible to become proud.
You can know Hebrew words.
You can quote theology.
You can teach Sunday school.
You can preach.
You can post Scripture every morning.
You can have thousands of followers who believe you are spiritually mature.
And still neglect your spouse.
Still entertain secret conversations.
Still feed pornography.
Still manipulate.
Still flirt.
Still nurture resentment.
Still become spiritually cold.
Still construct a private life completely different from your public Christianity.
Knowledge cannot substitute for obedience.
And neither can religious reputation.
Then the Old Testament gives marriage language an even greater theological depth.
Malachi 2:14 describes the wife as:
אֵשֶׁת בְּרִיתֶךָ
eshet beritekha—
“the wife of your covenant.”
There is the word:
בְּרִית — berit.
Covenant.
That changes everything.
Biblical marriage is more than a prolonged romantic mood.
Feelings matter enormously.
Affection matters.
Desire matters.
Tenderness matters.
Friendship matters.
But covenant says, “My faithfulness is not supposed to disappear every time my emotions change.”
This does not mean Scripture commands someone to silently remain in immediate danger or conceal abuse.
It never gives an abuser divine permission to terrorize a spouse.
Christian teachings about headship, submission, forgiveness, reconciliation, or covenant must never be twisted into weapons for coercion, violence, sexual abuse, threats, or control.
If you are in immediate danger, getting to safety and seeking appropriate help is not rebellion against God.
And forgiveness does not automatically mean immediate restoration of trust.
Trust can be shattered in minutes and rebuilt over a long period through truth, repentance, accountability, changed behavior, wisdom, and time.
This distinction matters because some Christians have been told that preserving the appearance of a marriage matters more than confronting evil inside it.
Scripture never calls darkness light merely because the darkness lives under a Christian roof.
But there is another mistake modern Christians make.
We sometimes read every difficult marriage as disposable.
Our culture can train us to treat covenant with the logic of consumerism.
If the product stops satisfying me, replace it.
If someone more exciting appears, upgrade.
If marriage becomes difficult, assume difficulty itself proves we chose incorrectly.
The Bible offers something far deeper.
Not endless tolerance of evil.
Not romanticized suffering.
Not pretending betrayal does not hurt.
But covenant faithfulness rooted in the character of a faithful God.
And then Jesus does something decisive.
When questioned about marriage in Matthew 19, Christ reaches past generations of human brokenness and points back to Genesis.
He quotes the creation pattern.
Male and female.
Leaving.
Holding fast.
One flesh.
In other words, Jesus does not use the later dysfunctions of Old Testament marriages as the definition of marriage.
He returns to the beginning.
That is crucial for understanding everything we have just read.
Abraham is not the standard.
Jacob is not the standard.
David is not the standard.
Solomon is certainly not the standard.
God’s design is the standard.
And ultimately, for Christians, marriage finds an even greater horizon in Christ.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5:25:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas.
“Husbands, love your wives.”
But Paul does not stop there.
He gives the terrifying measure of that love:
καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν
“As Christ loved the church.”
And what did Christ’s love look like?
A cross.
Self-giving.
Sacrifice.
Holiness.
Grace.
Truth.
Jesus did not love His people because they had performed well enough to deserve Him.
Romans tells us that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
That does not make sin irrelevant.
It makes grace astonishing.
This is where every Old Testament marriage eventually points us beyond itself.
Not because every marriage is a direct allegory of Jesus.
But because every broken human relationship exposes how desperately humanity needs redemption.
The Bible contains scandal after scandal.
Deception.
Jealousy.
Sexual sin.
Betrayal.
Manipulation.
Favoritism.
Idolatry.
Power abused.
Promises broken.
Families shattered.
And God did not hide any of it.
Why?
Because Scripture is not a public-relations campaign for human beings.
It is the story of a holy God dealing with sinful people and moving history toward redemption.
Then Jesus came.
Not as another flawed patriarch.
Not as another king corrupted by desire.
Not as another husband who failed his covenant.
Christ came as the faithful Bridegroom.
He loved His people unto death.
He carried sin to the cross.
He rose from the grave.
And now sinners who repent and believe are not merely given better relationship advice.
They are given new life.
That means there is hope for the husband who finally admits, “I have become cold.”
Hope for the wife who realizes bitterness has colonized her heart.
Hope for the couple who cannot remember how to speak without fighting.
Hope for the person who committed adultery and is finally willing to stop hiding.
Hope for the spouse devastated by betrayal who needs wisdom, safety, truth, and time.
Hope for the single Christian who has spent years believing marriage is the missing proof of God’s goodness.
Hope for the widow who still reaches toward the other side of the bed.
Hope for the divorced believer carrying shame into church every Sunday.
Hope even for the person reading this who knows that everyone thinks your marriage is fine.
But you know.
God knows.
There are things nobody else sees.
And perhaps the question is no longer, “How do I make my marriage look Christian?”
Perhaps the question is:
“What would happen if Jesus were actually allowed into the room I keep locked?”
Into the resentment.
Into the browser history.
Into the secret messages.
Into the financial deception.
Into the pride.
Into the emotional affair you insist is “just friendship.”
Into the fantasies.
Into the unforgiveness.
Into the silence.
Into the need to control.
Into the words you keep using as weapons.
Into the wounds you have refused to acknowledge.
Into the loneliness you are terrified to admit.
Marriage does not need better pretending.
It needs truth.
And sinners do not need better camouflage.
We need a Savior.
Maybe you have spent years blaming your spouse for everything.
Maybe your spouse has genuinely sinned against you.
Both things can sometimes be true: another person can be responsible for the evil they committed against you while God is simultaneously confronting something sinful inside your own heart.
Repentance is not accepting responsibility for someone else’s sin.
It is finally taking responsibility for yours.
That is one of the most liberating lessons buried inside these ancient marriages.
God works with real people.
Not Instagram marriages.
Not staged anniversary photographs.
Not couples who have learned how to smile through church.
Real people.
Abraham and Sarah had complications.
Isaac and Rebekah had dysfunction.
Jacob’s household was painfully fractured.
David created devastation.
Solomon possessed extraordinary wisdom and still wandered.
Yet through this deeply imperfect history, God continued moving His redemptive promise forward until, in the fullness of time, Jesus Christ came.
That is not permission to sin.
It is evidence that human sin cannot defeat God’s redemptive purposes.
And maybe that is exactly what somebody needs to hear tonight.
Your failure does not have to write the final sentence.
Your betrayal does not have to become your identity.
Your wounds do not have to become your god.
Your marital status does not determine your worth.
Your past does not possess authority greater than the blood of Jesus Christ.
But grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus does not merely cover our scandal so we can continue producing more of it.
He calls us to repent.
To turn.
To confess.
To forgive.
To seek wisdom.
To make restitution where appropriate.
To pursue holiness.
To tell the truth.
To put sin to death.
To love sacrificially.
To become, by the power of the Spirit, different people.
That is the difference between cheap religious sentiment and the Gospel.
The Gospel does not say, “What you did doesn’t matter.”
The Gospel says sin mattered enough that Christ went to the cross.
And grace is powerful enough that sin does not have to own you anymore.
So perhaps tonight the most spiritual thing you can do is not post another Bible verse.
Maybe it is putting the phone down and telling your spouse:
“I was wrong.”
Maybe it is confessing something you have hidden.
Maybe it is seeking pastoral counsel and qualified professional help.
Maybe it is establishing boundaries where serious harm has occurred.
Maybe it is choosing faithfulness when nobody would ever know if you compromised.
Maybe it is finally admitting that you cannot heal your marriage through willpower.
Maybe your prayer tonight is only:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
That prayer is not too small.
The tax collector in Jesus’ parable could barely lift his eyes toward heaven.
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
And Jesus said that man went home justified.
This is Christianity.
Not impressive people proving themselves worthy of God.
Sinners coming empty-handed to Christ.
Be truthful. You can simply comment, “Jesus, change me.”
If your marriage is hurting and you do not know what comes next, comment, “Pray for us.”

And if you are single, widowed, divorced, or waiting, you are not a secondary Christian. Marriage is not the Gospel. Jesus is. Your completeness is not postponed until another human being chooses you.

Not because every sentence will apply today, but because covenant gets difficult, memories get selective, emotions become loud, and sometimes we need to return to truth when feelings are trying to rewrite it.
Not as an accusation toward your spouse. Not as a passive-aggressive message aimed at somebody.
And consider sending this privately to the person who would never publicly admit that they are struggling.
Salvation is by grace. The Gospel is not for sale.
Supporting Gospel work, however, can be one voluntary expression of Christian generosity and stewardship when done freely and joyfully.
Save what you may need again.
Follow so you can continue growing with us.
And above everything else, go back to Jesus.
Because the greatest lesson from the marriages of the Old Testament is not that good people always build perfect families.
They did not.
It is that humanity has always been desperately capable of turning covenant into chaos when the human heart wanders from God.
Yet across generations of flawed husbands, wounded wives, complicated families, terrible decisions, shattered trust, repentance, mercy, judgment, and astonishing grace, God kept writing.
He kept moving history toward Bethlehem.
Toward Calvary.
Toward an empty tomb.
Toward Jesus.
And perhaps He is confronting your story now.
Not because every marriage will end the way we want.
Not because every broken relationship will necessarily be restored.
Not because repentance erases every earthly consequence.
But because nobody who comes to Jesus in repentance and faith has to remain the person sin made them.
The Bible never promised you a scandal-free human story.
It revealed something better:
a Savior powerful enough to redeem sinners inside one.
Your worst chapter may explain how you arrived here—but only Jesus has the authority to write who you become next.
